<script type="application/ld+json">{"@context": "https://schema.org","@type": "NewsArticle","headline": "What’s Behind China’s Trouble on the Afghanistan-Tajikistan Border?","description": "An interview with Edward Lemon on the recent attacks targeting Chinese workers near the Afghanistan-Tajikistan border.","image": [{"@context": "https://schema.org/","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl":"https://thediplomat.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/sizes/td-story-s-2/thediplomat_2025-12-10-225855.jpg","creditText": "Johnny van der Leelie on Unsplash","copyrightNotice": "Unsplash","license": "https://unsplash.com/license","acquireLicensePage": "https://unsplash.com/photos/brown-and-gray-mountain-painting-h3a7hMonbBI","representativeOfPage": "True" }], "datePublished": "2025-12-10T22:55:00Z","dateModified": "2025-12-10T23:11:57Z","copyrightYear": "2025","author": [{"@type": "Person", "name": "Catherine Putz", "url": "https://thediplomat.com/authors/catherine-putz/"}],"publisher": {"@id": "https://thediplomat.com/#publisher","name": "The Diplomat","legalName": "Diplomat Media Inc.","description": "Asia-Pacific’s leading current affairs magazine.","url": "https://thediplomat.com","email": "support@thediplomat.com","logo": { "@type": "ImageObject", "url": "https://thediplomat.com/wp-content/themes/td_theme_v3/assets/logo/diplomat_logo_amp.jpg", "width": 600, "height": 60 },"sameAs": [ "https://www.facebook.com/diplomatmagazine", "https://twitter.com/Diplomat_APAC", "https://www.linkedin.com/company/the-diplomat" ]},"isAccessibleForFree": "False","hasPart": { "@type": "WebPageElement", "isAccessibleForFree": "False", "cssSelector" : ".jsonld-markup-paywall-content" },"articleBody": "In late November 2025, over the span of four days, there were two separate cross-border attacks targeting Chinese workers in Tajikistan near the Afghan border. At least five Chinese nationals were killed, according to government and media reports.  Chinese workers have been targeted in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border area and in Pakistan’s Balochistan Province – but the borders with Central Asia have not been the sites of such attacks until recently. In the following interview, Edward Lemon – president of the Oxus Society for Central Asian Affairs and a research assistant professor at The Bush School of Government and Public Service, Texas A&M University, Washington D.C. – lays out what is known about the recent attacks, how they fit into Tajikistan’s difficult relationship with the Taliban in Afghanistan and China’s hesitance to become too deeply involved in the region’s security, even as its interests grow. What sets the recent attacks on Chinese workers in the Afghanistan-Tajikistan border area apart from previous attacks on Chinese interests in the wider South and Central Asian region? This is the second set of incidents in Tajikistan within the space of a year in which Chinese citizens have been killed on the Tajik side of the border. Last year's incident (in the same district along the Tajik-Afghan border as the November 25, 2025 incident) was the first time a Chinese citizen was killed in Tajikistan. The November 25 incident was the deadlier of the two, with three killed.  While in the 2024 incident it was unclear that the Chinese citizens were the target, the recent attacks on both sides of the border appear to have been targeted. These incidents are certainly unprecedented for Tajikistan. But there have been a spate of such attacks in Afghanistan and Pakistan in recent years in which Chinese companies and workers have been targeted. If the recent incidents become a pattern and we see more Chinese workers targeted, this will force China to place more pressure on the Tajik and Afghan governments to ensure security and could result in more security assistance and Chinese private security companies expanding their presence in both countries. The motivation for the attacks is unclear at this juncture, with various authorities using terms like “criminal groups,” and “terrorists,” but without naming any specific outfits. What do you think the possible motivations behind the attacks could be? The motivations are not clear. No group has claimed responsibility. It does appear that the [attacking] groups were drug traffickers. One theory is that the attack was retaliation against the Tajik border forces for a successful raid they conducted, with Chinese technology, against Afghan smugglers the week before.  Tajikistan had been hesitant to engage with the Taliban in the immediate aftermath of its return to power in August 2021, but that stance appears to have shifted. In the context of the recent attacks, the Taliban claim to have dispatched a delegation to Tajikistan, although Dushanbe did not confirm the visit. Do you think these attacks will motivate closer engagement between Tajik authorities and the Taliban? Tajikistan's relations with the Taliban have been difficult, to say the least. [Tajikistan's President] Rahmon has been critical of the new government, arguing it discriminates against ethnic Tajiks and supports terrorist organizations, in particular Jamaat Ansurallah, which was established by citizens of Tajikistan and aims to topple the government in Dushanbe. But there are pragmatic reasons for cautious engagement. Tajikistan sells electricity to Afghanistan. Both sides benefit from the illegal smuggling of narcotics, gemstones, and other products. We have seen the reopening of cross border markets and a few, underreported, meetings between officials in recent months. The recent incidents, however, are more likely to cause a rift as the attackers emanated from the Afghan side. The Tajik government would like the Taliban to contain violence within its own borders. More incidents like this could derail the rapprochement. On November 30, soon after the second attack, Taliban authorities announced the arrest of two individuals. To what extent are these kinds of attacks a liability for the Taliban government in its relations with China? Similarly, do these attacks put Tajikistan’s relations with China at risk? These kinds of incidents are embarrassing for both sides, especially Afghanistan. They want to present the impression that they can provide security and stability in order to attract investments. These attacks tarnish that image and are clearly causing concern in Beijing.  A number of foreign governments – including China, the U.S., Russia, the EU – have funded various programs directed at border security in Tajikistan over the last quarter-century. To what extent have these efforts yielded meaningful improvements? If not, why have they failed to make a difference? Outside actors have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into border security along the Tajik-Afghan border. China has built border posts and funded facilities. Western donors have built bridges and checkpoints. Russia had its own guards stationed on the border until 2005 and still has advisors in the country.  While the border has not seen mass violence since the early 2000s, this is less the result of effective border enforcement and more about the stabilization of the situation in Tajikistan and Afghanistan. The Tajik border service remains underfunded and deeply corrupt. It is one of the main actors in the smuggling of drugs across the border, making it resistant to change and reliant on the continued flow of illicit goods. Russia maintains a military base in Tajikistan and was once more actively engaged in security along the frontier with Afghanistan. China, it has been reported, now maintains some security infrastructure in the region too. Is either country prepared – in both practical and political terms – to be a true security guarantor in the region? China's facility is in a remote corner of Tajikistan, far from smuggling routes. It is more symbolic than anything. China is a hesitant actor in the region. It has increased its security role, but wants to avoid becoming entangled in costly conflicts. It is more likely to rely on increased security assistance and private security companies than on any kind of intervention.  Russia is better positioned to act as a guarantor. It has around 7,500 troops stationed in the country and has a treaty obligation under the Collective Security Treaty to protect Tajikistan should there be an armed incursion. It is more likely than China to actually intervene. But only if there is a large scale destabilization, which remains unlikely at present.","inLanguage": "en"}</script>

		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">In late November 2025, over the span of four days, there were two separate cross-border attacks </span><a href="https://thediplomat.com/2025/12/5-chinese-workers-killed-in-2-attacks-in-tajikistan-along-afghan-border/"><span style="font-weight: 400;">targeting Chinese workers in Tajikistan near the Afghan border</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;">. At least five Chinese nationals were killed, according to government and media reports. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Chinese workers have been targeted in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border area and in Pakistan’s Balochistan Province – but the borders with Central Asia have not been the sites of such attacks until recently. In the following interview, Edward Lemon – president of the Oxus Society for Central Asian Affairs and a research assistant professor at The Bush School of Government and Public Service, Texas A&M University, Washington D.C. – lays out what is known about the recent attacks, how they fit into Tajikistan’s difficult relationship with the Taliban in Afghanistan and China’s hesitance to become too deeply involved in the region’s security, even as its interests grow.</span></p>
<p><b>What sets the recent attacks on Chinese workers in the Afghanistan-Tajikistan border area apart from previous attacks on Chinese interests in the wider South and Central Asian region?</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">This is the second set of incidents in Tajikistan within the space of a year in which Chinese citizens have been killed on the Tajik side of the border. Last year’s incident (in the same district along the Tajik-Afghan border as the November 25, 2025 incident) was the first time a Chinese citizen was killed in Tajikistan. The November 25 incident was the deadlier of the two, with three killed. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">While in the 2024 incident it was unclear that the Chinese citizens were the target, the recent attacks on both sides of the border appear to have been targeted. These incidents are certainly unprecedented for Tajikistan. But there have been a spate of such attacks in Afghanistan and Pakistan in recent years in which Chinese companies and workers have been targeted. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">If the recent incidents become a pattern and we see more Chinese workers targeted, this will force China to place more pressure on the Tajik and Afghan governments to ensure security and could result in more security assistance and Chinese private security companies expanding their presence in both countries.</span></p>
<p><b>The motivation for the attacks is unclear at this juncture, with various authorities using terms like “criminal groups,” and “terrorists,” but without naming any specific outfits. What do you think the possible motivations behind the attacks could be?</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">The motivations are not clear. No group has claimed responsibility. It does appear that the [attacking] groups were drug traffickers. One theory is that the attack was retaliation against the Tajik border forces for a successful raid they conducted, with Chinese technology, against Afghan smugglers the week before. </span></p>
<p><b>Tajikistan had been hesitant to engage with the Taliban in the immediate aftermath of its return to power in August 2021, but that stance appears to have shifted. In the context of the recent attacks, the Taliban claim to have dispatched a delegation to Tajikistan, although Dushanbe did not confirm the visit. Do you think these attacks will motivate closer engagement between Tajik authorities and the Taliban?</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Tajikistan’s relations with the Taliban have been difficult, to say the least. [Tajikistan’s President] Rahmon has been critical of the new government, arguing it discriminates against ethnic Tajiks and supports terrorist organizations, in particular Jamaat Ansurallah, which was established by citizens of Tajikistan and aims to topple the government in Dushanbe.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">But there are pragmatic reasons for cautious engagement. Tajikistan sells electricity to Afghanistan. Both sides benefit from the illegal smuggling of narcotics, gemstones, and other products. We have seen the reopening of cross border markets and a few, underreported, meetings between officials in recent months. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">The recent incidents, however, are more likely to cause a rift as the attackers emanated from the Afghan side. The Tajik government would like the Taliban to contain violence within its own borders. More incidents like this could derail the rapprochement.</span></p>
<p><b>On November 30, soon after the second attack, Taliban authorities announced the arrest of two individuals. To what extent are these kinds of attacks a liability for the Taliban government in its relations with China? Similarly, do these attacks put Tajikistan’s relations with China at risk?</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">These kinds of incidents are embarrassing for both sides, especially Afghanistan. They want to present the impression that they can provide security and stability in order to attract investments. These attacks tarnish that image and are clearly causing concern in Beijing. </span></p>
<p><b>A number of foreign governments – including China, the U.S., Russia, the EU – have funded various programs directed at border security in Tajikistan over the last quarter-century. To what extent have these efforts yielded meaningful improvements? If not, why have they failed to make a difference?</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Outside actors have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into border security along the Tajik-Afghan border. China has built border posts and funded facilities. Western donors have built bridges and checkpoints. Russia had its own guards stationed on the border until 2005 and still has advisors in the country. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">While the border has not seen mass violence since the early 2000s, this is less the result of effective border enforcement and more about the stabilization of the situation in Tajikistan and Afghanistan. The Tajik border service remains underfunded and deeply corrupt. It is one of the main actors in the smuggling of drugs across the border, making it resistant to change and reliant on the continued flow of illicit goods.</span></p>
<p><b>Russia maintains a military base in Tajikistan and was once more actively engaged in security along the frontier with Afghanistan. China, it has been reported, now maintains some security infrastructure in the region too. Is either country prepared – in both practical and political terms – to be a true security guarantor in the region?</b></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">China’s facility is in a remote corner of Tajikistan, far from smuggling routes. It is more symbolic than anything. China is a hesitant actor in the region. It has increased its security role, but wants to avoid becoming entangled in costly conflicts. It is more likely to rely on increased security assistance and private security companies than on any kind of intervention. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Russia is better positioned to act as a guarantor. It has around 7,500 troops stationed in the country and has a treaty obligation under the Collective Security Treaty to protect Tajikistan should there be an armed incursion. It is more likely than China to actually intervene. But only if there is a large scale destabilization, which remains unlikely at present.</span></p>
